problems.1: Lead time is wrong by a lasting margin in many sectors
problems.2: Housing's order side fails in most worlds while its output is right
problems.3: The order book, overdue orders and phantom orders go wrong together with lead time
problems.4: Unit cost has level errors, with bands that miss it
problems.5: Price errors follow the unit cost errors
problems.6: Machinery breaks down entirely in one world
problems.7: Oil and gas capacity pipeline and output disagree with official figures
problems.8: Sector inventories do not fit the data, and several order totals are unsettled
problems.9: The model's own bands are too narrow and rely on heavy widening

fixes.label: 1A
fixes.title: Add quoted lead-time readings in five more sectors
fixes.fix: Give tracked firms in Housing, Autos, Oil and gas, Wholesale and Food a monthly reading of the lead time they quote, as tracked Machinery and Semiconductors firms already have. Today lead time in these five sectors is set only by the model's equations, which is why its error stays the same in the observed history as at the nowcast. Each source's own bias is still estimated, so the readings can only fix a level error larger than that bias's range, and untracked firms stay unobserved.
fixes.test: A rebuilt bundle (same seeds) with the readings and a full rerun of every world; lead time's error on the Scorecard (15.3%) should fall and its 11 failing cells in Housing, Oil and gas, Autos, Wholesale and Food should drop, with Orders below 9.1%.

fixes.label: 1B
fixes.title: Hold waiting-time settings where nothing measures lead time
fixes.fix: In sectors with no lead-time reading, keep the sector's processing time and its variability factor at their starting values instead of letting the fit move them. Nothing in those sectors' data bears on these two settings, yet they set most of lead time where the order book is small (Wholesale, Food), so the fit can push them anywhere to help other quantities and leave a lasting lead-time offset. Part of any gain may come from the synthetic worlds being drawn around those same starting values, so it says less about real data.
fixes.test: Refits of Wholesale, Food, Housing, Autos and Oil and gas at all four dates on every world; lead time's Scorecard error (15.3%) and Wholesale's lead-time failures (2 of 5) should fall with no other cell getting worse.

fixes.label: 1C
fixes.title: Let the filter correct orders in Autos and Oil and gas
fixes.fix: Let the monthly filter adjust the order level and overdue orders of Autos and Oil and gas firms, as it already does for Machinery and Semiconductors. Their lead-time failures come in the same worlds as large order-book misses (Autos world 01: 50% and 55%; Oil and gas world 04: 61% and 48%), so a wrong order level that never gets corrected looks like the cause. The same change for Machinery raised its fit to data and cut its error against the truth by a third.
fixes.test: Refits of Autos and Oil and gas at all four dates on every world; their lead-time and order-book cells on the Scorecard (Autos 30.8% and 16.7%, Oil and gas 32.0% and 19.2%) should fall, and so should their failures.

fixes.label: 2A
fixes.title: Add the official backlog of homes sold not built
fixes.fix: Add the official monthly count of new homes sold but not yet completed as a reading of Housing's whole order book. Today the only backlog readings come from three listed builders each quarter, and completions say how many homes are finished, not how many are waiting, so the untracked builders' backlog is free to drift. A whole-sector backlog reading did exactly this for Machinery and Semiconductors, covering the firms no one reports on.
fixes.test: Housing refitted at all four dates on each world rebuilt with the reading (other sectors' fits kept); Housing's Orders cell (26.3%, fails in 3 of 5) and its order book, lead time, overdue and phantom orders failures (11 cells) should fall.

fixes.label: 2B
fixes.title: Let the filter correct Housing's orders month by month
fixes.fix: Let the monthly filter adjust Housing's order level and overdue orders, as it does for Machinery. Housing's new orders grow less certain when data are added in every world (spread ratios 3.7 to 11.5), and in three worlds the backlog runs away while completions stay right, which is what an order level that nothing corrects would do. An earlier test of the order level alone left that spread ratio high but did cut Housing's error against the truth.
fixes.test: Housing refitted at all four dates on every world; Housing's Orders cell (26.3%) and its overdue orders (5.65 mo) should fall and fail in fewer than 3 of 5 worlds.

fixes.label: 2C
fixes.title: Keep the best of three Housing fits
fixes.fix: Fit Housing three times at each date from different starts, keep the fit that best predicts observations held back from fitting, and finish it on all the data from there. Housing fails in worlds 01, 03 and 05 and is nearly perfect in 02 and 04, the pattern of a fit that sometimes lands in the wrong place; choosing this way avoided bad fits in Wholesale and Machinery before.
fixes.test: Three Housing fits per date with a held-out check on every world; Housing's Orders cell should fall from 26.3% and its failures from 2.8 per world, most of all in worlds 01 and 03.

fixes.label: 3A
fixes.title: Let stocked-out copies recover their inventory
fixes.fix: Remove the filter rule that stops adjusting a simulated copy's finished stock for good once it has run out with orders late. On an earlier world this had a large side effect: overdue orders in Oil and gas and Machinery stopped running away and the error against the truth fell by about a third with the same fits. The runaway overdue and phantom orders here (Housing world 03 at 17 months of output, Machinery world 03 at 3.4) look like the same stuck copies.
fixes.test: The filter rerun with the bundle's existing fits on every world and date; overdue orders on the Scorecard (Housing 5.65 mo, Machinery 0.83 mo, Autos 0.48 mo) and the near-zero group (0.41 mo) should fall, with failures below 7 per world.

fixes.label: 3B
fixes.title: Cap how much long waits inflate new orders
fixes.fix: Lower the ceiling on how far a long lead time can inflate new orders, from ten times the normal lead time to about twice. Buyers who see long waits place extra orders, which lengthen the book and the wait further; a copy that enters this loop feeds phantom orders into overdue orders and lead time, as Housing world 03 shows (phantom orders 10.9 months of output). The worlds stay well clear of that range, so the cap should only stop runaway copies.
fixes.test: Refits of Housing, Autos, Oil and gas and Machinery on every world; phantom and overdue orders on the Scorecard (Housing 2.79 mo and 5.65 mo) and Orders (9.1%) should fall.

fixes.label: 4A
fixes.title: Add companies' reported cost of goods sold
fixes.fix: Add the cost of goods sold, or gross margin, that listed companies report each quarter to their observations in every sector. Today nothing measures a firm's unit cost: it is inferred from price and revenue, so a wrong starting cost is matched by a wrong markup and never corrected, which fits errors that stay flat at every horizon with bands that miss them. Untracked firms would still lean on their group's average.
fixes.test: A rebuilt bundle (same seeds) with the reports and a full rerun of every world; unit cost's error (5.2%) and its failures (Autos world 01, Machinery world 03) should fall, with price following.

fixes.label: 4B
fixes.title: Start each firm's unit cost from its own price
fixes.fix: Start each firm's unit cost at its first observed price less the sector's normal markup, and narrow how far the fit may move it from there. The starting cost is now allowed to wander a whole log unit, and in world 03 it was recovered 1.75 starting ranges off in Machinery; a start tied to observed prices would leave less room for a wrong cost to be offset by a wrong markup.
fixes.test: Refits of Autos, Machinery, Housing and Food on every world; unit cost and price on the Scorecard (Autos 16.8% and 11.0%, Machinery 11.1% and 15.5%) should fall without the core group rising.

fixes.label: 4C
fixes.title: Let price readings correct a lasting cost level
fixes.fix: Give each copy a lasting unit-cost level that the filter can adjust from price readings, as it adjusts the order level, so a cost that starts wrong can be moved month by month. Because markup is pulled back toward its normal level, a lasting price gap would gradually be read as cost. It helps only firms whose prices are observed.
fixes.test: A full rerun of every world; unit cost's Scorecard error (5.2%) should fall and its error 12 months ahead should no longer equal the nowcast's.

fixes.label: 5A
fixes.title: Add official price indexes for Machinery, Autos and Housing
fixes.fix: Give Machinery, Autos and Housing an official monthly price index as a whole-sector price reading that may move only unit cost and markup, as Wholesale's index now does. Their prices fail in the worlds where unit cost fails, and the untracked firms, most of each sector, have no price reading at all. An index tracks changes better than levels, so it may correct drift more than a wrong starting level.
fixes.test: The three sectors refitted on each world rebuilt with the indexes; price on the Scorecard (Machinery 15.5%, Housing 12.7%, Autos 11.0%) and its 3 failing cells should fall, and unit cost with it.

fixes.label: 5B
fixes.title: Use one normal markup per sector
fixes.fix: Estimate one normal markup for each sector instead of one per firm, so cost and markup cannot trade off firm by firm. The fit recovered the starting markup a full starting range off in Housing world 03, the other side of its unit cost error, and by the stricter measure markup is learned from a firm's own data for only about one firm in ten. A similar sharing of other settings earlier did not help, so this is uncertain.
fixes.test: Refits of Autos, Machinery, Housing and Food on every world; price and unit cost on the Scorecard should fall in those sectors, most of all in the worlds where they fail.

fixes.label: 6A
fixes.title: Keep the best of three Machinery fits
fixes.fix: Fit Machinery three times at each date from different starts, keep the fit that best predicts observations held back from fitting, and finish it on all the data from there. Machinery's collapse is in one world, as one bad fit would be, and on an earlier world this choice cut Machinery's error against the truth from 0.50 to 0.14, though its agreement with official production did not improve.
fixes.test: Three Machinery fits per date with a held-out check on every world; Machinery's failing cells in world 03 (finished inventory, overdue orders, price, unit cost, order book) should pass, with its other worlds no worse.

fixes.label: 6B
fixes.title: Anchor untracked Machinery firms to official production
fixes.fix: Set the overall size of Machinery's untracked firms from the official production statistic during fitting, as 11 other sectors already do. On an earlier world this took Machinery's agreement with official production from 40 to 99 in 100 months and roughly halved its error against the truth on two sets of random numbers; here world 03's output is 32.5% off that statistic.
fixes.test: Machinery refitted at all four dates on every world; Machinery's core cell (6.5%) and its world 03 failures should fall, and its official production row on Sector totals against official statistics should agree in most months.

fixes.label: 7A
fixes.title: Fit Oil and gas without official stock readings
fixes.fix: Fit Oil and gas's parameters without the official petroleum stock readings and use them only in the monthly filter. On an earlier world this cut Oil and gas's error against the truth from 0.28 to 0.11, mostly by removing a fit that blew up, and improved its agreement with official production; the stock readings pull the fit toward stocks the model cannot reach. It was never adopted.
fixes.test: Oil and gas refitted at all four dates on every world; its Orders (18.4%) and Inputs and pipeline (12.0%) cells should fall, and official production should agree in more months in worlds 02, 03 and 05.

fixes.label: 7B
fixes.title: Keep the best of three Oil and gas fits
fixes.fix: Fit Oil and gas three times at each date, keep the fit that best predicts held-back observations, and finish it on all the data starting from that fit rather than refitting from scratch. On an earlier world the chosen fits themselves cut Oil and gas's error against the truth from 0.28 to 0.03, but refitting from scratch lost most of it. World 04's miss of half the capacity under construction looks like one bad fit.
fixes.test: Three Oil and gas fits per date with a held-out check on every world; Oil and gas's order book, capacity announced and under construction in world 04 (47.6%, 44.2%, 50.0%) should pass.

fixes.label: 7C
fixes.title: Add a sector-wide count of active drilling rigs
fixes.fix: Add the weekly industry count of active drilling rigs, taken monthly, as a reading of Oil and gas's whole-sector capacity under construction. Rig activity is observed today only for tracked producers, so the untracked ones' pipeline rests on the model; a whole-sector reading would cover them, as the backlog surveys do for Machinery and Semiconductors.
fixes.test: Oil and gas refitted on each world rebuilt with the reading; capacity under construction (13.3%) and announced (18.1%) on the Scorecard should fall, most of all in world 04.

fixes.label: 8A
fixes.title: Use a filter update that cannot widen
fixes.fix: Replace the filter's random perturbation of each reading with the deterministic form of the same update, which can only narrow the copies' spread. With 100 copies, the random perturbation and chance links between a reading and unrelated quantities can push copies apart, which would explain order totals that grow less certain when data are added. The Scorecard's footprint of this problem is small (Retail's finished inventory in one world).
fixes.test: A full rerun of every world; spread ratios above 1.2 on What the data pin down should become rare, and the Scorecard's Orders (9.1%) and near-zero group (0.41 mo) should not get worse.

fixes.label: 8B
fixes.title: Let sector-wide readings move only what they measure
fixes.fix: Extend the rule adopted for Wholesale's margin index, which may now change only unit cost and markup, to the other whole-sector readings such as official production, sales and inventories: each may move only the quantities it measures and their direct inputs. A sector inventory reading that also moves capacity or orders through chance links can leave both stock and orders wrong; for Wholesale this rule cut the error against the truth.
fixes.test: A full rerun of every world; sector inventories on Observations against the model should fall in range more often (32 to 60 in 100 now), and Retail's finished inventory and the Scorecard's Orders group should improve.

fixes.label: 9A
fixes.title: Recalibrate range widening by quantity on older worlds
fixes.fix: Set one widening factor per quantity and horizon instead of one for all, calibrated on earlier synthetic worlds rather than this bundle, so lead time is widened less and unit cost more. A single factor of 2.31 cannot both cover level errors and stay sized elsewhere. A similar test before helped capacity but lowered other quantities on a world whose revisions differed.
fixes.test: The filter's published bands rebuilt for every world with the new factors; Scorecard coverage should stay near 90% while unit cost's coverage rises above its near-zero level and lead time's falls below 100%.

fixes.label: 9B
fixes.title: Widen ranges less where data pin a quantity
fixes.fix: Scale the extra widening of each sector total by how much the data narrow it: little where a quantity is pinned, the full amount where it comes mostly from the model. The widening stands in for parameter uncertainty that the copies do not carry, which matters most where data say little. An earlier split showed lead time's ranges too wide even where data inform it, so this may not reach lead time.
fixes.test: The published bands rebuilt for every world; Scorecard coverage should move toward 90% from 94% with no group's error changed, and model-driven quantities should keep their coverage.
